title: Reading link previews before you click
body_md:
## Hover. Read. Then decide.

The single highest-leverage habit in this entire course is also the simplest: before you click any link, see where it actually goes. Five seconds, every time, and you avoid the majority of credential-harvest attacks.

The mechanics are slightly different on each platform, but the move is always the same.

### Desktop browser

Hover the link without clicking. Look at the bottom-left corner of the browser window. Almost every browser displays the destination URL there. Read the registered domain.

### Email client (desktop)

Same trick — hover the link in the message, the destination appears in a tooltip or status bar. If you don't see it, your client is hiding it. Most clients let you toggle that on.

### Mobile (iOS / Android)

Long-press the link instead of tapping. A preview card appears showing the actual URL. On iOS, the preview includes a thumbnail and the full destination. On Android, the preview shows the URL plus options.

### Shortened links (bit.ly, t.co, tinyurl.com)

Short URLs deliberately hide their destination. They are unsafe to click without an unshortener. Useful free tools include:

- **unshorten.it** — paste the short URL, see the real destination.
- **checkshorturl.com** — same idea, slightly different ecosystem.

In 2024 onward, any unexpected short URL from a brand you trust should be treated as untrusted until you've unshortened it.

### QR codes

A QR code is just a URL in barcode form. When you scan a QR code with a modern phone, it shows you the URL *before* opening it. **Read the preview**. If the destination doesn't match the brand, don't open.

## Two patterns to learn by heart

1. **The phishing redirect.** A link that looks like `https://secure-paypal.com/verify` may actually redirect through three intermediate hops before landing on the credential-harvest page. Modern browsers show the *final* URL in the address bar after redirects — so always re-check the address bar after the page loads, not just the link you clicked.
2. **The genuine-looking host with attacker-controlled path.** A URL like `https://docs.google.com/forms/abc123` is hosted by Google, but the *form content* is anything the attacker wanted. Brand-name hosts don't make their content safe. The host tells you who's hosting; it doesn't tell you who wrote what's on the page.

widget_config.question: You hover over a link in an email from your bank. The destination URL shown at the bottom of your browser is `https://bit.ly/3KhPq2X`. What is the correct next move?

choices.text: Click the link — your bank uses URL shorteners for security.
choices.explanation: Major banks generally do not use bit.ly-style shorteners for transactional emails — both because it makes phishing detection harder and because it would damage their own trust. A shortener in a bank email is itself a yellow flag.

choices.text: Open the bank's app or website by typing the address yourself; ignore the link.
choices.explanation: Correct, and this is the safest move regardless of how the URL looks. You have a known good path to your bank already — use it. The link in the email is suspect until proven otherwise, and proving it requires unshortening *and* a domain check.

choices.text: Forward the email to a colleague and ask their opinion.
choices.explanation: Better than clicking, but you've increased the chance that *they* click the link by accident. Always include 'don't click — just look' in any forward like this. The cleaner action is still to verify through your own known channel.

choices.text: Use an unshortener tool to see the real URL, then decide.
choices.explanation: Acceptable, but more work than necessary when you already have a trusted path to the bank. Save the unshortener for cases where there's no easier verification route.

widget_config.hint: What's the cheapest correct action? You already have a verified path to your bank.
